# select in futures_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures-util/^0.3.30/macro.select.html

```
macro_rules! select {
    ($($tokens:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
**crate features**only.

`async-await-macro` and `async-await` and `std`## Expand description

Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. If multiple futures are ready,
one will be pseudo-randomly selected at runtime. Futures directly
passed to `select!` must be `Unpin` and implement `FusedFuture`.

If an expression which yields a `Future` is passed to `select!`
(e.g. an `async fn` call) instead of a `Future` by name the `Unpin`
requirement is relaxed, since the macro will pin the resulting `Future`
on the stack. However the `Future` returned by the expression must
still implement `FusedFuture`.

Futures and streams which are not already fused can be fused using the
`.fuse()` method. Note, though, that fusing a future or stream directly
in the call to `select!` will not be enough to prevent it from being
polled after completion if the `select!` call is in a loop, so when
`select!`ing in a loop, users should take care to `fuse()` outside of
the loop.

`select!` can be used as an expression and will return the return
value of the selected branch. For this reason the return type of every
branch in a `select!` must be the same.

This macro is only usable inside of async functions, closures, and blocks.
It is also gated behind the `async-await` feature of this library, which is
activated by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use futures::future;
use futures::select;
let mut a = future::ready(4);
let mut b = future::pending::<()>();
let res = select! {
    a_res = a => a_res + 1,
    _ = b => 0,
};
assert_eq!(res, 5);
```
```
use futures::future;
use futures::stream::{self, StreamExt};
use futures::select;
let mut st = stream::iter(vec![2]).fuse();
let mut fut = future::pending::<()>();
select! {
    x = st.next() => assert_eq!(Some(2), x),
    _ = fut => panic!(),
}
```
As described earlier, `select` can directly select on expressions
which return `Future`s - even if those do not implement `Unpin`:

```
use futures::future::FutureExt;
use futures::select;
// Calling the following async fn returns a Future which does not
// implement Unpin
async fn async_identity_fn(arg: usize) -> usize {
    arg
}
let res = select! {
    a_res = async_identity_fn(62).fuse() => a_res + 1,
    b_res = async_identity_fn(13).fuse() => b_res,
};
assert!(res == 63 || res == 13);
```
If a similar async function is called outside of `select` to produce
a `Future`, the `Future` must be pinned in order to be able to pass
it to `select`. This can be achieved via `Box::pin` for pinning a
`Future` on the heap or the `pin!` macro for pinning a `Future`
on the stack.

```
use core::pin::pin;
use futures::future::FutureExt;
use futures::select;
// Calling the following async fn returns a Future which does not
// implement Unpin
async fn async_identity_fn(arg: usize) -> usize {
    arg
}
let fut_1 = async_identity_fn(1).fuse();
let fut_2 = async_identity_fn(2).fuse();
let mut fut_1 = Box::pin(fut_1); // Pins the Future on the heap
let mut fut_2 = pin!(fut_2); // Pins the Future on the stack
let res = select! {
    a_res = fut_1 => a_res,
    b_res = fut_2 => b_res,
};
assert!(res == 1 || res == 2);
```
`select` also accepts a `complete` branch and a `default` branch.
`complete` will run if all futures and streams have already been
exhausted. `default` will run if no futures or streams are
immediately ready. `complete` takes priority over `default` in
the case where all futures have completed.
A motivating use-case for passing `Future`s by name as well as for
`complete` blocks is to call `select!` in a loop, which is
demonstrated in the following example:

```
use futures::future;
use futures::select;
let mut a_fut = future::ready(4);
let mut b_fut = future::ready(6);
let mut total = 0;
loop {
    select! {
        a = a_fut => total += a,
        b = b_fut => total += b,
        complete => break,
        default => panic!(), // never runs (futures run first, then complete)
    }
}
assert_eq!(total, 10);
```
Note that the futures that have been matched over can still be mutated
from inside the `select!` block’s branches. This can be used to implement
more complex behavior such as timer resets or writing into the head of
a stream.

---

# select_biased in futures_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures-util/^0.3.30/macro.select_biased.html

```
macro_rules! select_biased {
    ($($tokens:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
**crate features**only.

`async-await-macro` and `async-await`## Expand description

Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. Unlike [ select!](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html), if multiple futures are ready,
one will be selected in order of declaration. Futures directly
passed to

`select_biased!` must be `Unpin` and implement `FusedFuture`.If an expression which yields a `Future` is passed to `select_biased!`
(e.g. an `async fn` call) instead of a `Future` by name the `Unpin`
requirement is relaxed, since the macro will pin the resulting `Future`
on the stack. However the `Future` returned by the expression must
still implement `FusedFuture`.

Futures and streams which are not already fused can be fused using the
`.fuse()` method. Note, though, that fusing a future or stream directly
in the call to `select_biased!` will not be enough to prevent it from being
polled after completion if the `select_biased!` call is in a loop, so when
`select_biased!`ing in a loop, users should take care to `fuse()` outside of
the loop.

`select_biased!` can be used as an expression and will return the return
value of the selected branch. For this reason the return type of every
branch in a `select_biased!` must be the same.

This macro is only usable inside of async functions, closures, and blocks.
It is also gated behind the `async-await` feature of this library, which is
activated by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use futures::future;
use futures::select_biased;
let mut a = future::ready(4);
let mut b = future::pending::<()>();
let res = select_biased! {
    a_res = a => a_res + 1,
    _ = b => 0,
};
assert_eq!(res, 5);
```
```
use futures::future;
use futures::stream::{self, StreamExt};
use futures::select_biased;
let mut st = stream::iter(vec![2]).fuse();
let mut fut = future::pending::<()>();

    x = st.next() => assert_eq!(Some(2), x),
    _ = fut => panic!(),
}
```

which return `Future`s - even if those do not implement `Unpin`:

```
use futures::future::FutureExt;

// Calling the following async fn returns a Future which does not
// implement Unpin

    arg
}

    a_res = async_identity_fn(62).fuse() => a_res + 1,
    b_res = async_identity_fn(13).fuse() => b_res,

```

a `Future`, the `Future` must be pinned in order to be able to pass
it to `select_biased`. This can be achieved via `Box::pin` for pinning a
`Future` on the heap or the `pin!` macro for pinning a `Future`
on the stack.

```

use futures::select_biased;

// implement Unpin
async fn async_identity_fn(arg: usize) -> usize {
    arg
}
let fut_1 = async_identity_fn(1).fuse();
let fut_2 = async_identity_fn(2).fuse();
let mut fut_1 = Box::pin(fut_1); // Pins the Future on the heap
let mut fut_2 = pin!(fut_2); // Pins the Future on the stack
let res = select_biased! {
    a_res = fut_1 => a_res,
    b_res = fut_2 => b_res,
};
assert!(res == 1 || res == 2);
```
`select_biased` also accepts a `complete` branch and a `default` branch.
`complete` will run if all futures and streams have already been
exhausted. `default` will run if no futures or streams are
immediately ready. `complete` takes priority over `default` in
the case where all futures have completed.
A motivating use-case for passing `Future`s by name as well as for
`complete` blocks is to call `select_biased!` in a loop, which is
demonstrated in the following example:

```

let mut b_fut = future::ready(6);

loop {
    select_biased! {
        a = a_fut => total += a,
        b = b_fut => total += b,
        complete => break,
        default => panic!(), // never runs (futures run first, then complete)
    }
}
assert_eq!(total, 10);
```
Note that the futures that have been matched over can still be mutated
from inside the `select_biased!` block’s branches. This can be used to implement
more complex behavior such as timer resets or writing into the head of

# stream_select in futures_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures-util/^0.3.30/macro.stream_select.html

```
macro_rules! stream_select {
    ($($tokens:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
**crate features**only.

`async-await-macro` and `async-await` and `std`## Expand description

Combines several streams, all producing the same `Item` type, into one stream.
This is similar to `select_all` but does not require the streams to all be the same type.
It also keeps the streams inline, and does not require `Box<dyn Stream>`s to be allocated.
Streams passed to this macro must be `Unpin`.

If multiple streams are ready, one will be pseudo randomly selected at runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use futures::{stream, StreamExt, stream_select};
let endless_ints = |i| stream::iter(vec![i].into_iter().cycle()).fuse();
let mut endless_numbers = stream_select!(endless_ints(1i32), endless_ints(2), endless_ints(3));
match endless_numbers.next().await {
    Some(1) => println!("Got a 1"),
    Some(2) => println!("Got a 2"),
    Some(3) => println!("Got a 3"),
    _ => unreachable!(),
}
```

# try_join in futures_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures-util/^0.3.30/macro.try_join.html

```
macro_rules! try_join {
    ($($tokens:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
**crate features**only.

`async-await-macro` and `async-await`## Expand description

Polls multiple futures simultaneously, resolving to a [ Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html) containing
either a tuple of the successful outputs or an error.

`try_join!` is similar to [ join!](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html), but completes immediately if any of
the futures return an error.

This macro is only usable inside of async functions, closures, and blocks.
It is also gated behind the `async-await` feature of this library, which is
activated by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

When used on multiple futures that return `Ok`, `try_join!` will return
`Ok` of a tuple of the values:

```
use futures::try_join;
let a = async { Ok::<i32, i32>(1) };
let b = async { Ok::<i32, i32>(2) };
assert_eq!(try_join!(a, b), Ok((1, 2)));
// `try_join!` is variadic, so you can pass any number of futures
let c = async { Ok::<i32, i32>(3) };
let d = async { Ok::<i32, i32>(4) };
let e = async { Ok::<i32, i32>(5) };
assert_eq!(try_join!(c, d, e), Ok((3, 4, 5)));
```
If one of the futures resolves to an error, `try_join!` will return
that error:

```
use futures::try_join;
let a = async { Ok::<i32, i32>(1) };
let b = async { Err::<u64, i32>(2) };
assert_eq!(try_join!(a, b), Err(2));
```

# inotify_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/inotify-sys/0.1.7/target-redirect/inotify_sys/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#inotify-bindings-for-the-rust-programming-language)inotify bindings for the Rust programming language

Please note that these are direct, low-level bindings to C functions that
form the inotify C API. Unless you have a specific reason to use this crate,
[inotify-rs](https://crates.io/crates/inotify), which is an idiomatic wrapper, is a much better choice.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

In general, inotify usage follows the following pattern:

- Create an inotify instance using `inotify_init``inotify_init1`
- Manage watches with `inotify_add_watch``inotify_rm_watch`
- Read event using `read`
- Close the inotify instance using `close`

Please refer to the [inotify man page](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/inotify.7.html) and the rest of this documentation
for full details.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [inotify_](https://docs.rs/struct.inotify_event.html)- event
- Describes a file system event

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_ACCESS.html)- ACCESS
- Event: File was accessed
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_ALL_EVENTS.html)- ALL_ - EVENTS
- Event: Any event occured
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_ATTRIB.html)- ATTRIB
- Event: Metadata was changed
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_CLOEXEC.html)- CLOEXEC
- Set the `FD_CLOEXEC`flag for an inotify instance
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_CLOSE.html)- CLOSE
- Event: File was closed
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE.html)- CLOSE_ - NOWRITE
- Event: Non-writable file or directory was closed
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_CLOSE_WRITE.html)- CLOSE_ - WRITE
- Event: Writable file was closed
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_CREATE.html)- CREATE
- Event: File or directory was created in watched directory
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_DELETE.html)- DELETE
- Event: File or directory in watched directory was deleted
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_DELETE_SELF.html)- DELETE_ - SELF
- Event: Watched file or directory was deleted
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_DONT_FOLLOW.html)- DONT_ - FOLLOW
- Don’t dereference path, if it is a symbolic link
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_EXCL_UNLINK.html)- EXCL_ - UNLINK
- Ignore events for children, that have been unlinked from watched directory
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_IGNORED.html)- IGNORED
- Indicates that a file system watch was removed
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_ISDIR.html)- ISDIR
- Indicates that the subject of an event is a directory
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_MASK_ADD.html)- MASK_ - ADD
- Update existing watch mask, instead of replacing it
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_MASK_CREATE.html)- MASK_ - CREATE
- Only create watches, errors on existing watches.
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_MODIFY.html)- MODIFY
- Event: File was modified
- [IN_MOVE](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_MOVE.html)
- Event: File or directory within watched directory was moved
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_MOVED_FROM.html)- MOVED_ - FROM
- Event: File or directory was moved out of watched directory
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_MOVED_TO.html)- MOVED_ - TO
- Event: File or directory was moved into watched directory
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_MOVE_SELF.html)- MOVE_ - SELF
- Event: Watched file or directory was moved
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_NONBLOCK.html)- NONBLOCK
- Set an inotify instance to non-blocking mode
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_ONESHOT.html)- ONESHOT
- Remove watch after one event
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_ONLYDIR.html)- ONLYDIR
- Only watch path, if it is a directory
- [IN_OPEN](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_OPEN.html)
- Event: File or directory was opened
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_Q_OVERFLOW.html)- Q_ - OVERFLOW
- Indicates that the event queue has overflowed
- [IN_](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_UNMOUNT.html)- UNMOUNT
- Indicates that file system containing a watched object has been unmounted

# inotify_add_watch in inotify_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/inotify-sys/^0.1.5/fn.inotify_add_watch.html

```
pub unsafe extern "C" fn inotify_add_watch(
    fd:
```
[c_int](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ffi/primitives/type.c_int.html),
    pathname: [*const ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)[c_char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ffi/primitives/type.c_char.html),
    mask: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
) -> [c_int](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ffi/primitives/type.c_int.html)## Expand description

Adds or updates an inotify watch

Adds an item to the watch list of an inotify instance, or modifies an item on that list. This function takes the following arguments:

- `fd`is the file descriptor of the inotify instance (created by- `inotify_init`- `inotify_init1`
- `pathname`is the path of the file or directory watch
- `mask`defines the behavior of this function and configures the watch

The following flags in `mask` control the type of events to watch for:

- `IN_ACCESS`
- `IN_ATTRIB`
- `IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE`
- `IN_CLOSE_WRITE`
- `IN_CREATE`
- `IN_DELETE`
- `IN_DELETE_SELF`
- `IN_MODIFY`
- `IN_MOVED_FROM`
- `IN_MOVED_TO`
- `IN_MOVE_SELF`
- `IN_OPEN`

The following constants can be used as shortcuts to set multiple event flags:

In addition, the following flags can be set to control the behaviors of the watch and this function:

The function returns `-1` if an error occured. Otherwise, it returns a
watch descriptor that can be used to remove the watch using
[ inotify_rm_watch](https://docs.rs/fn.inotify_rm_watch.html) or identify the watch via

[’s [wd`] field.](https://docs.rs/struct.inotify_event.html)

`inotify_event`Please refer to the [man page](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/inotify_add_watch.2.html) for additional details.

# inotify_rm_watch in inotify_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/inotify-sys/^0.1.5/fn.inotify_rm_watch.html

## Expand description

Removes an inotify watch

Removes an item from the watch list of an inotify instance. The inotify
instance is identified by the `fd` argument. The watch is identified by
the `wd` argument.

Returns `0` on success, `-1` on failure.

Please refer to the [man page](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/inotify_rm_watch.2.html) for additional details.

# inotify_event in inotify_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/inotify-sys/^0.1.5/struct.inotify_event.html

## Expand description

Describes a file system event

From [inotify(7)](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/inotify.7.html):

To determine what events have occurred, an application

[read(2)](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/read.2.html)s from the inotify file descriptor. If no events have so far occurred, then, assuming a blocking file descriptor,[read(2)](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/read.2.html)will block until at least one event occurs (unless interrupted by a signal, in which case the call fails with the error EINTR; see[signal(7)](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal.7.html)).Each successful

[read(2)](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/read.2.html)returns a buffer containing one or more of this structure.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.wd)

`wd: `[c_int](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ffi/primitives/type.c_int.html)Identifies the watch for which this event occurs

This is one of the watch descriptors returned by a previous call to
[ inotify_add_watch()](https://docs.rs/fn.inotify_add_watch.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.mask)

`mask: `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)Describes the type file system event

One of the following bits will be set, to identify the type of event:

- `IN_ACCESS`
- `IN_ATTRIB`
- `IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE`
- `IN_CLOSE_WRITE`
- `IN_CREATE`
- `IN_DELETE`
- `IN_DELETE_SELF`
- `IN_IGNORED`
- `IN_MODIFY`
- `IN_MOVED_FROM`
- `IN_MOVED_TO`
- `IN_MOVE_SELF`
- `IN_OPEN`
- `IN_Q_OVERFLOW`
- `IN_UNMOUNT`

Some constants cover multiple bits, and can be used for a less precise check of the event type:

In addition, the [ IN_ISDIR](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_ISDIR.html) bit can be set.

A number that connects related events

Currently used only for rename events. A related pair of
[ IN_MOVED_FROM](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_MOVED_FROM.html) and

[events will have the same, non-zero, cookie. For all other events, cookie is 0.](https://docs.rs/constant.IN_MOVED_TO.html)

`IN_MOVED_TO`[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.len)

`len: `[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)The length of `name`

Used to determine the size of this structure. When `name`
isn’t present (`name` is only present when an event occurs
for a file inside a watched directory), it is 0. When `name`
*is* present, it counts all of `name`’s bytes, including `\0`.

The

`name`field is present only when an event is returned for a file inside a watched directory; it identifies the file pathname relative to the watched directory. This pathname is null-terminated, and may include further null bytes (‘\0’) to align subsequent reads to a suitable address boundary.

The `name` field has been ommited in this struct’s definition.

# IN_CLOEXEC in inotify_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/inotify-sys/^0.1.5/constant.IN_CLOEXEC.html

`pub const IN_CLOEXEC: `[c_int](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ffi/primitives/type.c_int.html) = libc::O_CLOEXEC; // 524_288i32## Expand description

Set the `FD_CLOEXEC` flag for an inotify instance

Can be passed to [ inotify_init1](https://docs.rs/fn.inotify_init1.html) to set the

`FD_CLOEXEC` flag for the
inotify instance. This changes the behavior of file descriptor when
[execve(2)](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/execve.2.html)’d. From

[fcntl(2)](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fcntl.2.html):

If the FD_CLOEXEC bit is 0, the file descriptor will remain open across an

[execve(2)](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/execve.2.html), otherwise it will be closed.
